title: Data Access with Spring Data JPA

concepts.title: Entity Mapping and the Persistence Context
concepts.description: @Entity turns a plain Java class into a row-backed, identity-tracked object that Hibernate's persistence context watches for changes -- understanding that context, and the four states an entity can be in, explains both why you rarely call save() explicitly and why mutating a 'detached' entity can silently do nothing at all.
learningObjectives: Map a Java class to a database table using @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue, and optional @Table/@Column overrides.
Explain what the persistence context is and how it differs from an ordinary in-memory Java object graph.
Distinguish the transient, managed, detached, and removed entity states and identify which state a given entity is in from a code snippet.
Explain automatic dirty checking and why calling repository.save() on an already-managed entity is often a redundant no-op.
Predict and explain the bug that results from mutating a detached entity outside of any active transaction.
Explain why two lookups for the same entity id inside one persistence context return the exact same Java object reference.

sections.heading: From Plain Class to Mapped Table: @Entity, @Id, and Column Overrides
@GeneratedValue Strategies: Not Just a Formality
sections.body: `@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` delegates id generation to the database's own auto-increment column, which is simple and universally supported, but has a real cost worth knowing about: because the actual id value only exists after the row is physically inserted, Hibernate cannot batch multiple inserts together for `IDENTITY`-strategy entities -- each insert has to happen (and return its generated id) before the next one can even be prepared, which matters once you're inserting thousands of rows and care about throughput. `GenerationType.SEQUENCE`, by contrast, asks the database for values from a sequence object, and Hibernate can pre-allocate a batch of sequence values in memory (configurable via `allocationSize`) and hand them out to multiple pending inserts before any of them actually hit the database -- which is why `SEQUENCE` is generally the recommended choice for databases that support it (PostgreSQL, Oracle) when insert throughput matters. `GenerationType.AUTO` lets the JPA provider pick a strategy appropriate for the configured database dialect, which is a reasonable default for getting started but worth revisiting once performance actually matters.

sections.heading: The Persistence Context: A Live, Tracked Set of Objects, Not Just Data
sections.body:
The **persistence context** is maintained by an `EntityManager` -- Spring Data JPA repositories delegate to one under the hood, so you get its behavior even though you rarely interact with `EntityManager` directly. It is best understood as an in-memory identity map plus change tracker, scoped to a transaction (in a typical Spring Boot service, that means scoped to one `@Transactional` method call). Every entity loaded or newly persisted within that scope is registered in it, and this has a genuinely useful guarantee attached: looking up the same id again, within the same persistence context, returns the exact same Java object reference -- not a second, separately-read copy with equal field values. Two variables pointing at 'the same order' inside one transaction are, quite literally, pointing at the identical object in memory.

Every entity, at any moment, is in exactly one of four states:

- **Transient**: a plain `new Order(...)` that has never been associated with any persistence context. JPA knows nothing about it yet; it's an ordinary Java object.
- **Managed (persistent)**: registered in an active persistence context -- returned by `repository.findById(...)`, or passed to `repository.save(...)` for the first time. Field mutations on a managed entity are tracked automatically.
- **Detached**: was managed at some point, but its persistence context has since closed (its transaction ended). The object still exists in memory, with real field values you can still read and write through ordinary Java code, but nothing is tracking mutations to it anymore.
- **Removed**: marked for deletion within an active persistence context (via `repository.delete(...)` or `entityManager.remove(...)`); still a live Java object for the remainder of the transaction, but scheduled to disappear from the database at the next flush.

sections.heading: Automatic Dirty Checking: Why You Rarely Call save() Yourself

examples.title: Mapping an Entity With Explicit Column Overrides
examples.explanation: Without any overrides, Hibernate would already have derived a table name of `order` and a column name of `customer_email` for `customerEmail` on its own -- so the overrides here are deliberately explicit rather than strictly necessary in this specific case, which is exactly the point of showing them: `@Table(name = "orders")` pins the plural table name regardless of what Hibernate's naming strategy would have guessed, which matters the moment a schema is designed independently of the entity class (a common situation with an existing database) rather than generated from it. `nullable = false` and `length = 255` add real, DB-enforced constraints beyond what the Java type system alone provides -- a `String` field has no length limit in Java, but the generated `VARCHAR(255)` column does, and the database will reject an insert that violates either constraint, independently of any Bean Validation you might also apply to a request DTO before it ever gets this far.

examples.title: Dirty Checking in Action: An Update With No save() Call
examples.explanation: findById returns a managed entity -- it's registered in the persistence context tied to this @Transactional method's transaction the moment it's loaded. Calling order.setStatus(...) is an ordinary field mutation through an ordinary setter; nothing about that call involves Spring or Hibernate directly. But because `order` is still managed when the method returns, Hibernate's flush at transaction commit compares its current field values against the snapshot taken when it was loaded, notices `status` changed, and issues `UPDATE orders SET status = ? WHERE id = ?` automatically. Adding `orderRepository.save(order)` right after `setStatus(...)` would not change this behavior at all -- it would just hand back the same already-tracked reference, doing nothing the pending flush wasn't already going to do.

examples.title: The Detached-Entity Bug: A Mutation That Silently Never Persists
examples.explanation: getOrder's @Transactional method returns cleanly, and its transaction -- and the persistence context tied to it -- closes the instant that method returns. The `order` object handed back to the controller is therefore already detached by the time `ship(...)` receives it, even though the reference looks exactly as usable as ever. Calling `order.setStatus(OrderStatus.SHIPPED)` in the controller mutates a plain, untracked Java object -- no flush, no snapshot comparison, no UPDATE statement, ever. The bug is dangerous precisely because nothing throws: the endpoint returns 200 OK, the object in memory really does say SHIPPED if you inspect it right there, and only a later query against the actual database reveals that nothing changed. The fix is to move the mutation inside a transactional service method -- an updateStatus(id, newStatus) method structured like markShipped in the previous example -- rather than mutating an entity that has already left its transaction's persistence context.

misconceptions.description: Calling repository.save(entity) is what actually saves your changes to the database -- without calling it, mutations you make to an entity are always lost.
misconceptions.clarification: Within an active transaction, on an entity that is still managed, Hibernate's automatic dirty checking flushes changed fields to the database at commit time with no explicit save() call needed at all -- save() on an already-managed entity is a redundant no-op that just returns the same tracked instance. Mutations are only ever silently lost when the entity is detached -- meaning it was loaded in one transaction that has already ended, and mutated later outside any active persistence context. In that specific situation, save() genuinely does real work (a merge), which is exactly where the kernel of truth in this misconception comes from -- it's true for detached entities, and irrelevant for managed ones.

misconceptions.description: The persistence context is basically just a performance cache -- turning it off, or not thinking about it, would only make things slower, not change what your code actually does.
misconceptions.clarification: The persistence context does provide caching (repeated lookups by id within one transaction avoid redundant SELECTs), but its identity-map and dirty-checking behavior are functional, not just performance optimizations. The identity guarantee -- two lookups for the same id inside one context return the literal same object -- affects correctness anywhere your code compares entity references or relies on one mutation being visible through every reference to 'the same' entity. Automatic dirty checking is what makes plain field mutations persist at all without any save() call; losing that (by operating on a detached entity, for instance) doesn't just run slower, it silently stops persisting changes altogether. Treating the persistence context as 'just a cache' is exactly the assumption that leads to the detached-entity bug above.

exercises.prompt: Customers report that clicking 'Mark as Shipped' returns success, but orders never actually show as shipped when they check back later. Find the bug in this code and fix it so the status change is actually persisted.
hints: getOrder's transaction ends the moment that method returns -- what state does the Order object end up in by the time the controller receives it?
Mutating a field on a detached entity is ordinary Java field assignment; nothing is watching for that mutation to flush it anywhere.
Move the fetch-and-mutate logic into a single @Transactional service method, so the entity is still managed at the moment its status is changed.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original getOrder is @Transactional(readOnly = true), so its persistence context closes the instant it returns -- the Order handed to the controller is already detached before ship(...) ever mutates it. Setting order.setStatus(...) in the controller is a plain, untracked field write: no snapshot exists to compare against, no flush is scheduled, and nothing persists, with no error raised anywhere to reveal the problem. The fix adds a dedicated markShipped method, itself @Transactional, that loads the order and mutates it within one single transaction -- so the entity is still managed at the exact moment its status changes, and Hibernate's automatic dirty checking picks up the change and flushes an UPDATE at commit. The controller now delegates the whole fetch-and-mutate operation to that one transactional method instead of pulling a managed entity out of its transaction and mutating it afterward.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Both findById calls happen inside the SAME @Transactional method -- are they using the same persistence context, or two separate ones?
The persistence context acts as an identity map: looking up the same id twice within one context doesn't re-read a second, separate copy.
If first and second are literally the same object, then mutating one through 'first' is visible through 'second' too -- there's nothing to actually re-fetch.
exercises.expectedAnswer: true, then SHIPPED. Both findById calls happen inside the same transaction, so they share one persistence context's identity map -- the second lookup for the same id returns the exact same managed object as the first, not a freshly re-read copy. Because first and second are the same object, mutating status through first is immediately visible when reading it through second.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both calls to orderRepository.findById(orderId) execute within the same @Transactional method, so they operate against the same persistence context. The first call loads the entity and registers it in that context's identity map, keyed by id. The second call, for the same id, does not issue a second independent load that produces a second object -- the persistence context recognizes it already has a managed entity for that id and simply returns the same reference. So `first == second` prints true: they are not merely equal-by-value, they are the identical object in memory. Because of that, first.setStatus(OrderStatus.SHIPPED) mutates the one and only Order object both variables point to, so reading second.getStatus() immediately afterward reports SHIPPED -- there was never a second object to have gone stale.

assessments.prompt: Inside an active @Transactional method, a field on a managed entity is mutated through its setter, and repository.save() is never called. What happens when the transaction commits?
options: Nothing persists, because save() was never called.
Hibernate's automatic dirty checking compares the entity's current state against its loaded snapshot, detects the change, and issues an UPDATE at flush time with no save() call required.
An exception is thrown at commit time because a managed entity was mutated without an explicit save() call.
The change only persists if the entity also has an @DynamicUpdate annotation.
assessments.explanation: As long as the entity stays managed (registered in an active persistence context) through the moment of mutation, Hibernate's dirty checking automatically detects the changed field against its baseline snapshot and issues the corresponding UPDATE at flush/commit time -- no save() call is required for a managed entity. Option A describes what happens to a DETACHED entity, not a managed one -- the distinction is exactly the point of this concept. Option C is false; mutating a managed entity without calling save() is completely ordinary and expected, not an error condition. Option D is a distractor; @DynamicUpdate changes which columns appear in the generated UPDATE statement (only the changed ones, versus all of them), it has nothing to do with whether the update happens at all.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer is confused: sometimes editing a field on an Order object they got back from a service method updates the database automatically, and other times an identical-looking edit does nothing at all, with no error. Explain what's actually going on, in terms of the entity's state and the persistence context's lifecycle.
assessments.modelAnswer: The difference has nothing to do with how the field is edited -- setStatus(...) looks and behaves identically either way -- and everything to do with whether the entity is still 'managed' at the moment the edit happens. A managed entity is one that is currently registered in an active persistence context: typically, this means it was loaded (or newly saved) inside a method that is still running inside its own @Transactional boundary. While an entity is managed, Hibernate keeps a snapshot of its field values from when it became managed, and at the moment that transaction commits (or an earlier flush happens), it compares the entity's current values against that snapshot and automatically issues an UPDATE for anything that changed -- no save() call needed, because the tracking and flushing are automatic side effects of the transaction's lifecycle, not of any particular method call. The moment that transactional method returns and its transaction commits, though, the persistence context tied to it closes, and every entity that was managed inside it -- including the very same object reference that's still sitting in a variable somewhere in the calling code -- becomes detached. It's still a perfectly normal, readable, writable Java object; nothing about calling a setter on it fails. But there is no longer any persistence context watching it, no snapshot being compared, and no flush that will ever pick up that mutation, because the transaction that would have done so is already finished. So the practical rule is: if you need a mutation on an entity to actually reach the database, that mutation needs to happen while the entity is still managed -- inside the same @Transactional method where it was loaded (or explicitly re-attached via save()/merge() if it's already detached) -- not on a reference you happened to keep around after that method already returned.

concepts.title: Spring Data JPA Repositories and Query Methods
concepts.description: Spring Data JPA generates a working repository implementation at application startup purely from an interface's method names and @Query annotations, eliminating hand-written DAO boilerplate -- and knowing when a derived query method is enough versus when you need JPQL or a native query is what keeps that convenience from becoming a source of startup failures and unreadable method names.
learningObjectives: Extend JpaRepository and explain what Spring Data generates from it without any implementation code being written.
Write derived query methods using findBy/existsBy/countBy naming conventions with And, Or, comparison, and OrderBy keywords.

Explain that Spring Data JPA parses a derived query method's name at application startup, not at call time, and predict the resulting exception when a method name references a property the entity doesn't have.
Write a @Query using JPQL and explain how JPQL's entity-and-field-oriented syntax differs from table-and-column-oriented SQL.
Use nativeQuery = true and explain the concrete situations where dropping to native SQL is necessary or preferable.
Choose correctly between a derived query method, JPQL, and a native query for a given data-access requirement.

sections.heading: JpaRepository: An Interface That Ships Its Own Implementation
Derived Query Methods: Parsing a Method Name Into a Query
@Query and JPQL: When a Method Name Isn't Enough
Native Queries: Escaping to Raw SQL, Deliberately
sections.body:
`@Query(value = "...", nativeQuery = true)` runs the given string as literal SQL against the underlying database, bypassing JPQL's entity-oriented translation layer entirely. This is the right tool specifically when you need something JPQL cannot express: a database-specific function (a PostgreSQL window function, a full-text search operator), a performance-tuned query shaped around a particular index or execution plan the ORM's abstractions would obscure, or a complex recursive/CTE query.

```java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT * FROM orders o
    WHERE o.total > :minTotal
    ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
    LIMIT 10
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Order> findTopRecentHighValueOrders(@Param("minTotal") BigDecimal minTotal);
```

The cost is real and worth weighing deliberately rather than reaching for `nativeQuery = true` out of habit: the query now refers to actual table and column names (`orders`, `created_at`), tying it to one specific schema and, in practice, often one specific database vendor's SQL dialect -- a `LIMIT` clause, for instance, is PostgreSQL/MySQL syntax, not standard SQL that every database understands the same way. You also lose some of JPQL's automatic entity-graph awareness; a native query mapped back onto an entity type generally works for simple, direct column-to-field mappings, but gets considerably more involved the moment you're trying to map a native query's result set onto a projection that spans multiple joined entities. The practical rule of thumb: reach for a derived method first, JPQL when a derived method's name would become unreadable or can't express the join/condition you need, and native SQL only when JPQL itself genuinely can't express what the database needs to do.

examples.title: A Repository Built Entirely From Derived Method Names
examples.explanation: None of these four methods have a body, and none needed one -- Spring Data JPA parses each method name into a query at startup by inspecting it against Order's mapped properties (customerEmail, status, total), confirms every referenced property genuinely exists, and generates a working proxy implementation before the application ever serves a request. findByStatusAndCustomerEmail requires both conditions to match (an implicit SQL AND); findByTotalGreaterThanOrderByTotalDesc adds a comparison keyword (GreaterThan) and a sort clause (OrderByTotalDesc) purely from vocabulary in the method name itself. existsByCustomerEmail returns a boolean rather than a list, generating an existence check rather than a full row fetch -- Spring Data recognizes exists/count/delete subjects and adjusts the generated query and return handling accordingly.

examples.title: A Startup Failure From a Typo'd Property Name
examples.explanation: Order's mapped fields are id, customerEmail, status, and total -- there is no customerName property anywhere on the entity. Spring Data JPA discovers this the moment it tries to parse findByCustomerName's name against Order's metamodel while building the repository proxy at startup, well before any HTTP request could ever call this method. It fails the entire application startup with PropertyReferenceException, naming the exact property it couldn't resolve (often with a helpful 'did you mean' suggestion, as shown). This is a deliberate, useful fail-fast behavior: a typo in a derived query method name is caught once, at startup, by every developer who runs the app locally or in CI, rather than being discovered later by whichever production request happens to be the first to call this specific method.

examples.title: JPQL With a Join, and the Native-SQL Equivalent
examples.explanation: The JPQL version's `join o.customer c` walks the mapped @ManyToOne (or similar) association on the Order entity by its Java field name, customer -- Hibernate translates this into whatever the actual foreign-key join looks like in the target database's SQL dialect, and the query never mentions customer_id or the customers table by name at all. The native version does exactly the same logical join but has to spell out the actual table (customers) and join column (customer_id) explicitly, and its status parameter is passed as a raw String rather than the OrderStatus enum, since native SQL has no awareness of JPA's entity-to-column type mapping the way JPQL does. Both return the same results here, but the JPQL version stays correct automatically if the underlying schema's join column is ever renamed (as long as the @ManyToOne mapping itself is updated to match) -- the native version would need to be edited by hand to track that same change.

misconceptions.description: A derived query method's name is just a suggestion to Spring Data -- if it's wrong or references a property that doesn't exist, you'll find out with a normal compiler error, the same way you would for a typo'd Java field access anywhere else.
misconceptions.clarification: A derived query method name is a plain String as far as the Java compiler is concerned -- it compiles successfully regardless of whether the properties it names actually exist on the entity, because the compiler has no idea method names are meant to be parsed as queries at all. The validation happens entirely at Spring Data JPA's own initialization step, when it builds the repository proxy by inspecting each method name against the entity's mapped properties -- and if that step fails, the result is an application that compiles cleanly but throws PropertyReferenceException and refuses to start. It's a real, hard failure, just one that surfaces at application startup rather than at compile time.

misconceptions.description: JPQL is basically just SQL with a slightly different name -- you can freely reference actual table and column names in a @Query string when a derived method name isn't expressive enough.
misconceptions.clarification: JPQL queries the entity model, not the database schema: `from Order o` refers to the Order entity by its class (or @Entity name), and property paths like `o.customer.email` navigate mapped Java fields and associations, not literal table and column names. Referring to a real table or column name inside a JPQL string generally just fails to resolve, because JPQL's parser is looking for entity and property names, not schema identifiers. Only a query explicitly marked nativeQuery = true is interpreted as literal SQL against the actual schema -- mixing the two mental models (schema-oriented thinking inside a plain @Query without nativeQuery = true) is a common, confusing mistake for anyone coming from writing raw SQL.

exercises.prompt: This Spring Boot application fails to start with 'PropertyReferenceException: No property 'email' found for type 'Order''. The Order entity has a field named customerEmail, not email. Find and fix the bug in this repository interface.
hints: Compare the property name embedded in the failing method's name against the actual field names declared on the Order entity.
Spring Data JPA parses findByEmail as 'find where the entity's email property equals the given argument' -- does Order actually have a field called exactly email?

Rename the method so the property name segment matches the entity's real field name, customerEmail, exactly -- the method's parameter name doesn't need to match, only the property name embedded in the method name does.
exercises.solutionExplanation: findByEmail tells Spring Data JPA to generate a query filtering on a property literally named email -- but Order's actual field is customerEmail, so there is no property named email anywhere on the entity's mapped model at all. Spring Data JPA discovers this mismatch while building the repository proxy at startup, before any request is ever served, and fails the whole application with PropertyReferenceException naming the unresolved property. Renaming the method to findByCustomerEmail makes the property segment of the method name match Order's real field exactly; the parameter name (email) is irrelevant to this resolution step -- only the property name embedded in the method name itself has to correspond to a real, mapped property, and once it does, the proxy builds successfully and the method works as intended.

exercises.prompt: Add a method to OrderRepository that finds all orders for a given customer email with a total greater than a given amount, sorted by total in descending order. Write it first as a derived query method, then write an equivalent version using @Query with JPQL.
hints: The derived method needs two ANDed conditions (customerEmail equals, total greater than) plus an OrderBy clause -- build the method name piece by piece using the And/GreaterThan/OrderBy...Desc vocabulary.

For the JPQL version, remember the query targets the Order entity and its property names (customerEmail, total), not table or column names -- use named parameters with :paramName and @Param to bind them.

Both versions should be logically equivalent -- if you're unsure the derived method name is correct, write out in English what it says ('find by customer email and total greater than, ordered by total descending') and check it against the requirement.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The derived method name is parsed piece by piece: findBy establishes a query, CustomerEmail matches the customerEmail property with equality, And joins a second condition, TotalGreaterThan matches the total property with a > comparison, and OrderByTotalDesc sorts results by total descending -- every piece of vocabulary in the name maps directly onto a clause in the generated query, and Spring Data JPA validates each property name (customerEmail, total) against Order's mapped fields at startup. The JPQL version expresses exactly the same logic explicitly: it selects Order entities, filters on the same two properties using named parameters bound via @Param, and sorts with an ordinary 'order by' clause -- readable as a single query string rather than assembled from name-parsing vocabulary, which becomes the more maintainable choice once a query like this needs to grow any further (an additional join, an OR condition, a subquery) than a derived method name can comfortably express.

assessments.prompt: A repository interface declares `List<Order> findByShippingCity(String city);`, but the Order entity has no property named shippingCity. When does this problem actually surface?
options: At compile time, because the Java compiler checks derived query method names against the entity's mapped properties.
At application startup, when Spring Data JPA builds the repository proxy and validates each derived method name against the entity's metamodel, throwing PropertyReferenceException.
The first time findByShippingCity is actually called at runtime, with a SQL error from the database.
It never surfaces as an error -- Spring Data JPA silently returns an empty list for any unresolvable property.
assessments.explanation: The Java compiler has no special knowledge of derived query method naming conventions -- it just sees a normal interface method declaration and compiles it without complaint, so option A is wrong. Spring Data JPA's own validation happens while it builds the repository's runtime proxy implementation during application startup, inspecting every declared method's name against the entity's actual mapped properties; an unresolvable property fails that step immediately with PropertyReferenceException, which is why the application never even finishes starting -- so option C (deferred to first call) and option D (silently returns empty) are both wrong; there is no silent or deferred failure mode here at all.

assessments.prompt: A developer defaults to writing every query as a derived method name, no matter how many conditions it needs, arguing that '@Query is just extra ceremony.' Explain the tradeoffs and when @Query (JPQL or native) is actually the better choice.
assessments.modelAnswer: Derived query methods are genuinely excellent for simple, one- or two-condition lookups -- findByCustomerEmail, existsByStatus, countByCustomerEmailAndStatus -- because the method name IS the query, fully readable at the call site, validated automatically against the entity's mapped properties at startup, and requiring zero query-string authoring or escaping. The tradeoff shows up as conditions accumulate: a method like findByStatusAndCustomerEmailAndCreatedAtAfterAndTotalGreaterThanOrderByCreatedAtDesc is technically valid and will work, but at that length it's genuinely harder to read accurately than the equivalent JPQL would be, and it becomes essentially impossible to express certain things at all through naming alone -- a join across multiple associations with a non-trivial condition, a subquery, an aggregate with a HAVING clause, or a query that needs to select a partial projection rather than a whole entity. @Query with JPQL solves exactly that gap: you write the query directly, as an actual query, keeping the same entity-and-property-oriented model (not raw table/column names) that keeps it reasonably database-portable and resilient to @Column renames, while being free to express joins, subqueries, and projections that a method name simply cannot encode. Native SQL, gated behind nativeQuery = true, is the further escape hatch reserved for the cases where even JPQL's abstraction can't reach -- a database-specific function, a query tuned around a specific index or execution plan, or syntax (like vendor-specific window functions) that has no JPQL equivalent at all -- accepting in exchange that the query now depends on the literal schema and, usually, one specific database vendor's dialect. The practical guidance is a spectrum, not a single rule: reach for derived methods while they stay readable, JPQL once they don't or once you need something method-name syntax can't express, and native SQL only when JPQL itself genuinely falls short of what the database needs to do.

concepts.title: Entity Relationships and the N+1 Query Problem
concepts.description: @OneToMany and @ManyToOne map foreign-key relationships between entities, but it's the fetching strategy behind them -- not the annotations themselves -- that determines whether loading a list of parents quietly issues one extra query per child collection, the N+1 problem, and fixing it requires understanding lazy loading, not just adding indexes.
learningObjectives: Map a bidirectional one-to-many/many-to-one relationship with mappedBy and explain which side owns the foreign key.
Explain the JPA-specified default fetch type for @ManyToOne versus @OneToMany and why they differ.
Explain precisely what causes the N+1 query problem and trace it through a concrete loop over a lazily-loaded association.
Fix an N+1 query using JOIN FETCH in JPQL or @EntityGraph, and explain the tradeoff of switching a relationship to eager fetching globally instead.
Explain LazyInitializationException and why it occurs specifically when an association is accessed after its persistence context has closed.
Predict the number of SQL queries a given code snippet involving lazily-loaded associations inside a loop will execute.

sections.heading: Owning Side vs. Inverse Side: What mappedBy Actually Does
Default Fetch Types: Why @ManyToOne Is EAGER but @OneToMany Is LAZY
sections.body:
The JPA specification gives `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` a default fetch type of `EAGER`, and gives `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` a default of `LAZY`. This isn't arbitrary: a `@ManyToOne` association points at exactly one related row -- loading an `OrderItem`'s `Order` is one additional row, cheap enough that fetching it immediately by default is a reasonable, low-risk assumption. A `@OneToMany` collection, by contrast, could be one row or could be ten thousand -- there's no way to bound it in advance, so JPA defaults to *not* loading it until something actually asks for it, which is exactly what `LAZY` means: the collection is populated with a proxy object at load time, and the real query that fetches its contents only fires the moment code actually calls a method on it (`.size()`, an iterator, `.get(0)`, anything that needs real data).

A genuinely common but harmful reaction to LAZY-related friction is to blanket-annotate every relationship `fetch = FetchType.EAGER` to 'make the problem go away.' This doesn't fix anything structurally -- it just moves the cost earlier and makes it unconditional: every single load of an `Order`, everywhere in the codebase, now always pulls its full `items` collection along with it, whether that specific code path needed it or not, and fetching multiple eagerly-loaded collections on one entity at once can itself trigger a Cartesian-product blowup in the generated SQL (covered further down). The right fix is almost always to keep collections LAZY by default and fetch eagerly *only at the specific query that actually needs the association*, which is exactly the tool `JOIN FETCH` and `@EntityGraph` provide.

sections.heading: The N+1 Problem: One Query Becomes N+1 Queries
sections.body:
Consider fetching a list of orders and then, for each one, reading its items:

```java
List<Order> orders = orderRepository.findAll();   // query #1: SELECT * FROM orders

for (Order order : orders) {
    System.out.println(order.getItems().size());  // one additional query PER order
}
```

`findAll()` issues exactly one query, returning `N` orders with their `items` collections populated as unfetched LAZY proxies -- no items have actually been loaded yet. The moment the loop calls `order.getItems().size()` on the first order, Hibernate has to go fetch that specific order's items right then, issuing `SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ?`. The same thing happens again for the second order, the third, and so on -- one additional query *per order*, for a total of `1 + N` queries where a single well-shaped query could have retrieved everything.

This is precisely why N+1 is such a notorious, recurring bug: with 3 orders in a local development database, this code runs in milliseconds and looks completely correct -- 4 queries is not something anyone notices. With 50,000 orders in production, it's 50,001 round trips to the database for what should have been one or two, and the resulting latency (or database connection pool exhaustion under load) is the first visible symptom, often long after the code that caused it was written, reviewed, and merged.

sections.heading: Fixing It: JOIN FETCH and @EntityGraph
LazyInitializationException: Accessing a Lazy Association After the Session Is Gone
sections.body:
A LAZY association's proxy is only usable while its owning entity is still managed -- which, tying directly back to the persistence-context lifecycle from the previous concept, means while the transaction that loaded it is still open. If an entity with an unfetched LAZY collection escapes its transaction (returned from a `@Transactional` service method to a controller, for instance) and something later calls `.getItems()` on it, there is no active session left to run the query the proxy needs -- and Hibernate throws `LazyInitializationException: failed to lazily initialize a collection, could not initialize proxy - no Session`, rather than silently returning an empty or stale collection.

This is a different failure mode from the silent detached-entity mutation bug in the previous concept -- this one is loud and immediate -- but it stems from the exact same root cause: code outside the transactional boundary trying to interact with something that only works *inside* it. The fix is the same pattern already established: either access the lazy association while still inside the transaction (map it to a DTO before the method returns, for instance, so the controller never touches the raw entity at all), or eagerly fetch exactly what you know you'll need via `JOIN FETCH`/`@EntityGraph` at the query that loads it, so there's no lazy proxy left to fail on later.

examples.title: A Correctly Mapped Bidirectional Relationship
examples.explanation: OrderItem.order, backed by @JoinColumn(name = "order_id"), is the owning side -- Hibernate writes to the order_id column based on what this field points to. Order.items, marked mappedBy = "order", is purely an in-memory, inverse view of that same relationship; it corresponds to no column of its own. addItem() exists specifically because mappedBy relationships require manual discipline: adding an item to the items list alone does NOT set that item's order field, and since order is the owning side, only a change to order actually gets persisted -- calling item.setOrder(this) explicitly is what makes the relationship, and therefore the eventual foreign-key value, actually correct. cascade = CascadeType.ALL means operations on the Order (like save or delete) cascade to its items automatically; orphanRemoval = true means removing an item from the items list (rather than reassigning it elsewhere) deletes that OrderItem row entirely, rather than leaving an orphaned row with a dangling reference.

examples.title: N+1 in Action: Counting Queries in a Loop
examples.explanation: findAll() issues one SELECT returning all Order rows, with each order's items collection populated as an unfetched LAZY proxy -- no order_items rows have been read yet at this point. The first call to order.getItems().size() inside the loop forces Hibernate to resolve that specific order's proxy, issuing a fresh SELECT ... FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ? -- and this repeats independently for every single order in the loop, because each order's items collection is its own separate, individually-lazy proxy. The query count scales linearly with the number of orders, which is exactly why this bug is invisible in small local datasets and only becomes an obvious, painful problem once real production data volume is involved.

examples.title: Fixing N+1 With JOIN FETCH
examples.explanation: join fetch o.items tells Hibernate to load each matching order's items collection in the SAME SQL query, via an actual SQL JOIN against order_items, rather than leaving it as a lazy proxy to be resolved later. Every order returned by findWithItemsByStatus already has its items collection fully populated by the time the method returns, so the loop's order.getItems().size() calls touch data that's already in memory -- no additional round trips to the database at all, regardless of how many orders are in the list. distinct matters here specifically because the join produces one result row per matched (order, item) pair -- an order with 4 items would otherwise appear 4 times in the raw JPQL result before entity de-duplication, and distinct filters that duplication out explicitly at the query level.

misconceptions.description: Setting fetch = FetchType.EAGER on every relationship is a safe, simple way to avoid LazyInitializationException and N+1 problems entirely.
misconceptions.clarification: Switching a relationship to EAGER globally doesn't eliminate the underlying cost of fetching that association -- it just makes the fetch happen unconditionally, on every single load of that entity, everywhere in the codebase, whether that particular code path needed the association or not. It can also create its own version of the N+1 problem (extra queries fire immediately and universally rather than only when actually accessed) or, when multiple eager collections are combined, a Cartesian-product blowup in the generated join. The actual fix is to keep the JPA-specified defaults (LAZY for collections) and fetch eagerly only at the specific query that needs the association, using JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph -- targeted, not global.

misconceptions.description: Since @OneToMany(mappedBy = ...) is just a mapping annotation, it doesn't matter which entity has mappedBy and which has @JoinColumn -- the resulting foreign key column ends up the same regardless of which side you put it on.
misconceptions.clarification: Exactly one side of a bidirectional relationship owns the foreign key -- conventionally, and almost always correctly, the @ManyToOne side, annotated with @JoinColumn naming the actual foreign-key column. The mappedBy side (@OneToMany) is purely an inverse, in-memory view with no column of its own; mappedBy's string value names the field on the OWNING side that this collection mirrors. Getting this backward, or omitting mappedBy on the @OneToMany side entirely, makes Hibernate treat the two annotations as describing two independent relationships rather than one relationship from two angles -- a common, confusing symptom being an unexpected extra join table appearing in the generated schema, or changes made through one side of the relationship never showing up when read through the other.

exercises.prompt: This method runs against a database containing 200 Author rows, each with a lazily-loaded books collection averaging 5 books. How many SQL queries does this method execute in total, and why?
hints: findAll() itself is exactly one query -- what does it actually populate for each author's books collection at that point: real data, or an unfetched proxy?
The @OneToMany default fetch type is LAZY -- when does the real query for one specific author's books actually fire?
Count one query for findAll(), plus one additional query for EVERY author whose books collection gets touched inside the loop.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 201 queries total: 1 for findAll() plus 1 more for each of the 200 authors, because author.getBooks() is a LAZY collection that only gets fetched with its own separate query the moment .size() is called on it, independently for every author in the loop.
exercises.solutionExplanation: findAll() issues exactly one SELECT that returns all 200 Author rows, with each author's books collection populated as an unfetched LAZY proxy -- no Book rows have been read at that point. The loop then calls author.getBooks().size() once per author; because @OneToMany defaults to LAZY, each of those calls independently triggers Hibernate to resolve that specific author's proxy with its own SELECT ... FROM books WHERE author_id = ? -- 200 separate queries, one per author, regardless of how many books each author actually has (the average of 5 books per author doesn't change the query COUNT, only the row count each of those 200 queries returns). Total: 1 (findAll) + 200 (one per author) = 201 queries -- the textbook N+1 shape, where N is the number of parent rows whose lazy collection gets touched.

exercises.prompt: This endpoint works correctly but is extremely slow in production with large datasets, even though it runs fine locally with a handful of test rows. Diagnose the N+1 problem and fix the repository method so the fix collapses the extra queries into the initial fetch.
hints: findByCountry issues one query; the stream's .map() then calls a.getBooks().size() for every single author returned -- what does that trigger, given books is a LAZY @OneToMany?
You need each author's books collection to already be populated by the time findByCountry returns, instead of being resolved lazily, one author at a time, inside the stream.
Add a query that eagerly loads books in the SAME query as the author lookup -- either @Query with JOIN FETCH, or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "books") layered onto the existing derived method.
exercises.solutionExplanation: findByCountry, as originally written, issues one query to fetch matching authors, but leaves each one's books collection as an unfetched LAZY proxy. The stream's a.getBooks().size() call then forces Hibernate to resolve that proxy separately for every single author in the result -- exactly the N+1 pattern, invisible with a few local test rows but severe once the country filter matches thousands of authors in production. Adding @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "books") to the same derived method tells Spring Data JPA to eagerly fetch the books association as part of the SAME query used to find authors by country, populating every returned author's books collection immediately -- so by the time the stream's .map() runs, no author's books collection is still a lazy, unresolved proxy, and the extra per-author queries disappear entirely. The derived method's name and behavior are otherwise unchanged; only the fetching strategy for this specific query was fixed.

assessments.prompt: Why does @ManyToOne default to EAGER fetching while @OneToMany defaults to LAZY?
options: It's an arbitrary historical default in the JPA specification with no real design reasoning behind it.

A @ManyToOne association points to exactly one related row, which is cheap to fetch by default; a @OneToMany collection could be arbitrarily large, so JPA defaults to not loading it until something actually accesses it.
@OneToMany defaults to LAZY only because Hibernate specifically overrides the JPA specification's default of EAGER for collections.
@ManyToOne is EAGER by default because lazy loading isn't technically possible for single-valued associations.
assessments.explanation: The defaults reflect a real cost/risk tradeoff specified by JPA itself: a @ManyToOne association resolves to exactly one additional row, a bounded and cheap cost to eagerly fetch by default. A @OneToMany collection has no such bound -- it could be empty or it could be tens of thousands of rows -- so JPA defaults to LAZY, deferring the cost until code actually needs the data. Option C is wrong; this is the JPA specification's own default, not a Hibernate-specific override. Option D is wrong; lazy loading of single-valued associations is technically possible (via bytecode enhancement or proxies) and JPA providers support it when explicitly requested -- it's simply not the DEFAULT for @ManyToOne.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says 'the app works fine in every test we've run, but production is somehow falling over under normal load' after a recent feature that lists parent entities along with a summary of their child collections. Explain what's most likely happening and how you'd confirm and fix it.
assessments.modelAnswer: This is the classic signature of the N+1 query problem, and the 'works fine in every test, falls over in production' symptom is almost a diagnostic fingerprint for it rather than a coincidence. If the new feature loads a list of parent entities and then, for each one, touches a lazily-loaded child collection (calling .size(), iterating it, or otherwise accessing it), each of those touches fires its own separate SQL query the first time it happens, because @OneToMany associations default to LAZY specifically so they're not fetched until something actually needs them. With a handful of rows in a local or test database, this produces a handful of extra queries -- fast enough that nobody notices, and functionally correct, since the DATA returned is exactly right; only the number of round trips to the database is wrong. In production, with real data volume, the same code executes one query per parent row instead of one query total, and that linear scaling in round trips -- not any logic bug -- is what causes slowness or connection pool exhaustion under real load. To confirm it, I'd enable SQL logging (or a query-count-asserting test, or a tool like Hibernate's statistics API) against a realistic-sized dataset and literally count the queries the endpoint issues -- seeing query count scale directly with the number of parent rows returned is the smoking gun. The fix is to change how the specific query that loads the parents fetches the association: adding JOIN FETCH to a JPQL query, or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "...") on a derived method, so the child collection is populated in the SAME initial query via a real SQL join, rather than fetched lazily and separately per parent. I'd deliberately avoid the tempting-but-wrong shortcut of just marking the association EAGER everywhere, since that fixes nothing structurally -- it just makes the same cost happen unconditionally on every load of that entity, everywhere in the codebase, rather than only where this specific feature actually needs it.
